initial_observation.encounter_context: urgently presented to a nearby hospital because of a femur fracture caused by an accident
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: She was alert on arrival but began to experience sleepiness approximately 5 hours later

evidence_items.source_text: A follow-up helical computed tomography (CT) of the brain revealed the absence of any additional severe lesions or skull fractures.
Chest CT confirmed an exudative lesion, and a pulmonary vascular computed tomography angiography (CTA) revealed no obvious abnormalities.

Total body CT revealed a left femoral comminuted fracture with dislocation (Fig. 1B). Her bilateral lung presented an exudative lesion as well as pleural effusion (Fig. 2A). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed diffuse abnormal signals in the bilateral cerebral hemisphere, brainstem, and cerebellum, which were suggestive of embolization (Fig. 3).
evidence_items.temporal_cue: on arrival to neurology department after 2 days

evidence_items.source_text: Immediate physical examination on arrival revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 4, a positive bilateral Babinski sign, a positive Kernig sign, and neck stiffness. The patients left thigh presented bruising and swelling and had been fixed with external fixation with restrained movement in the previous hospital (Fig. 1A). She presented an arterial pressure of 148/80 mm Hg, heart rate of 124 bpm, and partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) of 64 mm Hg. Her blood gas analysis revealed a pH value of 7.4.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: on arrival to neurology department after 2 days

evidence_items.source_text: Fourteen days after the fracture, both the lung symptoms and lung CT findings were considerably improved (Fig. 2B).
Transthoracic echocardiography ultrasound was performed again, and shunts through a PFO were observed (Fig. 4).
evidence_items.temporal_cue: 15 days after the fracture (the following day after lung CT improvement)

evidence_items.source_text: Under active supportive care and hormone therapy, the patient was finally discharged with dysphasia and an untreated closed fracture.
Combined with the patients trauma history and imaging findings of the lung and brain, the patient was initially diagnosed with FES, whose corresponding treatment is mainly supportive.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: on arrival to neurology department after 2 days
